introduction-the-pilot-and-the-engines.core: Every AWS service has a control plane (APIs that create, modify and delete resources: launching instances, changing DNS records) and a data plane (the resources doing the work: running instances, answering DNS queries). Data planes are simpler and more available; control planes are complex and fail more often.

first_principles.problem: A recovery plan depends on launching new instances during an outage, exactly when the EC2 APIs are degraded.
truths: Control planes have more logic and dependencies.
Data planes must keep running independently.
Outages often hit control planes first.
derivation: **Classify** each dependency as control or data plane.

analogy.title: A plane's pilot and its engines
analogy.story: If the radio to air traffic control fails, the engines keep flying the plane.
analogy.breaks: Pilots can improvise; systems must be designed in advance not to need the control plane.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: You know which parts to avoid in recovery.

check.q: Is changing a Route 53 record a control- or data-plane action?
check.a: Control plane; answering DNS queries is the data plane.

the-availability-gap.core: Control planes are typically less available than data planes because they involve more components, workflows, databases and validation. AWS designs data planes for higher availability, and SLAs often reflect that. Recovery mechanisms that need control planes inherit their lower availability during the very events that trigger them.

first_principles.problem: A team assumes failover will work because the service SLA is high, without noticing the failover uses an API call.
truths: More moving parts means lower availability.
Large events stress control planes (everyone calls APIs at once).
Data planes run with fewer dependencies.

analogy.title: A ticket office versus the trains
analogy.story: During a storm, the ticket office queue explodes while trains already running keep moving.
analogy.breaks: Ticket offices close visibly; control-plane degradation can be partial and confusing.

example.title: AZ failure response
flow: Plan A: launch replacement instances in other AZs (control plane, may throttle)
Plan B: run N+1 capacity across AZs already (data plane)

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Pay for headroom to avoid API dependency.

check.q: Why are control planes stressed during large outages?
check.a: Many customers simultaneously call APIs to recover, causing throttling and slowness.

the-cardinal-sin-control-plane-dependenc.core: The cardinal sin is making your data path depend on a control plane: calling IAM or describe APIs per request, looking up configuration through management APIs on every call, or requiring resource creation to serve traffic. When that control plane wobbles, your whole service fails even though the data plane is fine.

first_principles.problem: A service calls DescribeInstances on each request to discover peers, and goes down when EC2 APIs throttle.
truths: Per-request API calls amplify dependency.
Describe APIs have rate limits.
Cached state can serve during outages.
derivation: Use **data-plane discovery** (DNS, Cloud Map data plane).
**Fail static**: keep last known good config.

analogy.title: Calling head office to approve every sale
analogy.story: When their phone line is busy, every till in every shop stops.
analogy.breaks: Shops could take cash anyway; code only does what it was designed to do.

example.title: Fixing peer discovery
flow: After: refresh peer list every 60 s, keep last good
API outage: service keeps serving with cached peers

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Data path independent of the control plane.

points: No APIs in the hot path.

check.q: What should a service do if its config API becomes unavailable?
check.a: Keep running on the last known good configuration (fail static).

static-stability-the-holy-grail.core: A statically stable system keeps working during a dependency failure without needing to change anything. For example, running enough capacity across three AZs that losing one still leaves sufficient capacity, rather than relying on launching replacements. Stability comes from pre-provisioning and avoiding reactive control-plane actions.

first_principles.problem: An AZ outage requires autoscaling to launch 50% more instances, but launches are delayed for hours.
truths: Reacting requires working control planes.
Pre-provisioned capacity is already there.
Over-provisioning costs money but buys resilience.
derivation: **Pre-establish** connections, DNS records and failover routes.
**Health checks** shift traffic in the data plane.

analogy.title: A building with a backup generator already running
analogy.story: When the grid fails, lights stay on; no one needs to order a generator.
analogy.breaks: Generators cost fuel only when used; idle capacity costs money all the time.

example.title: Capacity across 3 AZs
flow: Lose 1 AZ → 300 remain → no action needed

check.q: How much capacity per AZ do you need across 3 AZs to survive one AZ loss statically?
check.a: 50% of total required load per AZ (150% overall).

case-study-route-53-and-the-100-sla.core: Route 53's DNS data plane is engineered for a 100% availability SLA: anycast across many edge locations, independent server fleets (shuffle sharding of name servers per zone) and static answers. Its control plane (changing records) lives in one region and is less available, so failover should rely on health checks (data plane), not record edits during an incident.

first_principles.problem: A DR runbook says 'update DNS to point at the DR region', which needs the Route 53 control plane during a crisis.
truths: DNS answers are served globally from the edge.
Record changes go through a central control plane.
Health checks run in the data plane.
derivation: Use **Application Recovery Controller routing controls** (highly available data-plane switches).

analogy.title: Pre-printed road diversion signs with automatic lights
analogy.story: When the road closes, sensors flip the lights; nobody needs to print new signs in the storm.
analogy.breaks: Road signs are local; DNS answers are cached by resolvers for the TTL.

example.title: Health-checked failover
flow: Primary record → us-east-1 ALB with health check
Primary unhealthy → DNS answers flip automatically
example.outcome: DNS failover that works in a crisis.

points: DNS answers are the data plane.

check.q: Why use health-checked failover records instead of editing DNS during an incident?
check.a: Health checks and answers are data-plane operations; editing records depends on the less available control plane.

the-big-red-button-problem.core: A 'big red button' manual failover sounds safe, but if pressing it calls control-plane APIs, deploys code or needs credentials from a dependent system, it may not work when needed. Design failover switches that are simple, pre-tested, data-plane based, highly available and protected against accidental or partial use.

first_principles.problem: During a regional outage, the failover script can't run because it needs IAM in the failed region and a CI pipeline that's also down.
truths: Failover tools have their own dependencies.
Rarely used tools rot.
Humans under stress make mistakes.
derivation: **Minimise dependencies** of the switch (ARC routing controls across 5 regions).

analogy.title: A fire alarm wired to the mains it's meant to protect
analogy.story: If the fire cuts the power, the alarm is silent.
mapping: Failover tool depending on failed region
analogy.breaks: Fire alarms are simple; failover often requires coordinated multi-step changes.

example.title: Dependency audit of a failover
flow: Script runs in CI (in failed region) ✗
Redesign: ARC routing control toggled via any of 5 regional endpoints ✓
example.outcome: a button that works when pressed.

check.q: What's the main risk of a manual failover script?
check.a: Its own dependencies (APIs, credentials, CI systems) may be impaired by the same outage.

limiting-the-blast-radius-cellular-archi.core: Cell-based architecture splits a service into independent, identical cells (full stacks), each serving a subset of customers, behind a thin routing layer. A bad deploy, poison request or overload affects only one cell, limiting blast radius. Shuffle sharding assigns customers to combinations of cells or nodes so two customers rarely share all resources.

first_principles.problem: One customer's malformed request crashes the shared fleet and takes down every customer.
truths: Shared everything means shared failure.
Independent copies contain faults.
Routing must be simpler than the cells.
derivation: Define a **cell** (full stack) with a max size.
Keep the **router thin** and highly available.
Use **shuffle sharding** for isolation between tenants.

analogy.title: Watertight compartments in a ship
analogy.story: A breach floods one compartment; the ship stays afloat.
analogy.breaks: Compartments are fixed; cells can be added as you grow.

example.title: Blast radius maths
flow: Shuffle sharding: two customers share all nodes with tiny probability

check.q: Why must the cell router be simpler than the cells?
check.a: It's shared by all cells; if it's complex, it becomes the single point of failure the cells were meant to avoid.
